lessons.title: Bullying, prejudice and being an upstander
lessons.bigQuestion: If you watch bullying and say nothing, are you part of it?
objectives: To understand how bullying and prejudice cause harm and how an upstander can safely help
successCriteria: Most: describe safe ways to be an upstander online and offline
Some: explain how UK law and Islamic teaching both oppose bullying
lessons.crossCurricular: Citizenship: the Equality Act 2010 and school anti-bullying duties

keywords.def: repeated, deliberate hurtful behaviour where there is an imbalance of power
an unfair opinion formed without reason or knowledge
someone who sees but does nothing
someone who acts safely to help

hook.text: If you watch bullying and say nothing, are you part of it?
hook.a: Silence can encourage the bully; safe action helps.

islamicLink.text: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Help your brother whether he is an oppressor or oppressed.' When asked how to help the oppressor, he said: 'By stopping him' (al-Bukhari). He also said whoever sees a wrong should change it with his hand, or his tongue, or at least hate it in his heart (Muslim).

starter.q: Name a TGA rule for live lessons.
starter.a: Camera on, chat for learning, no screenshots.
People are diverse so we know one another; nobility is by righteousness.

teach.heading: What is bullying?
teach.note: One-off unkindness is wrong but may not be bullying.

teach.heading: Prejudice and bullying
bullets: Prejudice: unfair views about a group
teach.note: Use fictional examples only.

teach.heading: Bystander or upstander
bullets: Do not join in or like it
teach.note: Safety first: never put yourself in danger.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Which is the safest upstander action in a group chat?
options: Screenshot, message the target kindly, tell an adult
check.why: It supports the target and lets adults act, without escalating.

practice.q: Is this bullying? A one-off joke someone found upsetting.
practice.a: Not bullying on its own (not repeated), but still unkind; apologise.
practice.model: Teacher checks the three features: repeated? deliberate? imbalance of power?

independent.q: Core: Scenarios (pupil PDF): decide if each is bullying and write an upstander action.
Extend: In the portal response box, write a short message to support a target of bullying.
independent.a: 'I saw what happened. It was not okay. I have told a teacher; you are not alone.'

independent.q: Stretch: Explain how the Equality Act 2010 and the hadith 'help your brother' both oppose prejudice-based bullying.
independent.a: The law protects characteristics like race and religion; the hadith commands stopping wrongdoing.

exit.q: Bullying is... A) one argument B) repeated, deliberate, with a power imbalance C) any disagreement
exit.a: B) repeated, deliberate, with a power imbalance
options: Repeated, deliberate, with a power imbalance

exit.q: Big question: if you watch bullying and say nothing, are you part of it? Explain.
exit.a: Silence can encourage it; a safe upstander action helps stop it.

lessons.homework: Write three upstander actions you could use online.
lessons.send: SEND: bullying checklist (repeated, deliberate, power). EAL: bystander, upstander, prejudice. Stretch: research the school's anti-bullying policy.

lessons.title: Peer influence and risky substances
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do some people do things in a group they would never do alone?
objectives: To understand how peer influence works and the risks and laws around vaping, smoking, alcohol and drugs
successCriteria: All: describe the health risks of vaping, smoking and alcohol
Most: state the UK laws on age limits and illegal drugs
Some: explain how peer influence works and use refusal strategies
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: drugs and their effects on the body

keywords.def: the effect friends and others our age have on our choices
an addictive drug in cigarettes and most vapes
being unable to stop doing or using something
the UK law that makes some drugs illegal

hook.text: Why do some people do things in a group they would never do alone?
hook.a: Wanting to fit in, fear of being left out, not wanting to look different.

islamicLink.text: Allah says intoxicants and gambling are 'defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it' (al-Ma'idah 5:90), and 'do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction' (al-Baqarah 2:195). The Prophet ﷺ said every intoxicant is khamr and every khamr is forbidden (Muslim).

starter.q: Name one way to respond to discrimination.

starter.a: Someone who acts safely to help.
Being unable to stop using something.

teach.heading: Risks
bullets: Smoking: cancer, heart and lung disease
Vaping: nicotine addiction; long-term effects still being studied
Alcohol: harms the developing brain, liver
teach.note: Factual, calm.

teach.heading: The law
bullets: Illegal to sell tobacco or vapes to under-18s
Illegal to sell alcohol to under-18s
Many drugs are illegal for everyone (Misuse of Drugs Act 1971)
teach.note: Possession of illegal drugs can lead to a criminal record.

teach.heading: How peer influence works
teach.note: Most young people do not vape or drink regularly: the 'everyone does it' idea is wrong.

teach.heading: Saying no
teach.note: Model a refusal.

model.problem: A friend offers a vape: 'Everyone's doing it.'
steps: Clear no: 'No thanks, I'm not into that.'
Reason: 'It's addictive and it's against my faith.'
Change subject: 'Want to play football instead?'
If pressure continues: leave and tell an adult

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: The legal age to buy alcohol or vapes in the UK is...
check.why: It is illegal to sell either to under-18s.

practice.q: Write a refusal line for 'Just try one sip.'
practice.a: 'No thanks, I don't drink.' and change the subject.
practice.model: Teacher writes a short refusal and a subject change.

independent.q: Core: Pressure scenarios (pupil PDF): write a refusal and an exit for each.
Extend: In the portal response box, explain why 'everyone does it' is misleading. Start: 'Most young people...'
independent.a: Most young people do not vape or drink regularly; influence makes it seem more common than it is.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain how Islamic teaching and UK law both protect young people from substances.
independent.a: Islam forbids intoxicants and self-harm; UK law sets age limits and bans some drugs.

exit.q: Nicotine is... A) a vitamin B) an addictive drug C) a type of water
Big question: why do people do things in a group they would not do alone?
exit.a: To fit in and avoid being left out: peer influence.

lessons.homework: Discuss with a parent: what would you do if offered a vape? Write your plan.
lessons.send: SEND: refusal phrases card. EAL: influence, addiction, refuse. Stretch: research recent UK laws on selling vapes.

lessons.title: Mental health: when feelings become too much
objectives: Recognise circumstances that can lead to intense emotions
Explain a range of healthy strategies and why some strategies are unhelpful
Assess whom, how and why to ask for support

keywords.def: persistent worry that is hard to control
feeling sad or flat for a long time
something that sets off a strong emotion
the people and services who can help you
trusting Allah after doing your best

starter: Name two people you could talk to when stressed.

teach.heading: When feelings become intense
bullets: Big events: exams, loss, conflict, change
Hormones and growing up affect mood
Feeling low or anxious sometimes is normal
Seek help if it lasts or stops daily life
teach.note: Say bismillah. Teach that everyone faces times of intense emotion: moving, a falling-out, exams, grief, illness. This lesson draws on the PSHE Association KS3 lesson ‘Healthy coping strategies’. Read the PSHE Association guidance ‘Preparing to teach about mental health’ before teaching. Do not ask for personal stories; use invented case studies. Keep language careful and avoid any detail of self-harm methods. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Unhelpful and helpful strategies
bullets: Unhelpful: bottling up, isolating, endless scrolling
Unhelpful: unkindness to others or risky habits
Helpful: talking, sleep, exercise, nature, creativity
teach.note: Use the invented case of Maryam, who stops replying to friends and stays up late scrolling after a bad test result. Ask: ‘Why might she do this? What are the short-term and long-term effects?’ Explain that unhelpful strategies may bring short-term relief but make things worse later. Pupils should identify a better plan for Maryam. Stress that if a strategy involves harming oneself, the right step is to tell a trusted adult.

teach.heading: Signs that someone needs support
bullets: Changes in sleep, appetite or energy
Feeling hopeless or very anxious for weeks
Feeling unsafe or thinking of self-harm: tell someone today
teach.note: Teach pupils to notice changes in themselves and in friends. Keep this factual and calm. Explain that physical symptoms can also be signs of worry. Stress that no one should have to cope alone and that a friend who is struggling needs an adult, not just a secret. Provide the line: ‘I am worried about you and I'm going to tell someone who can help because I care.’

teach.heading: Islamic perspectives on hardship and help
bullets: Qur'an 2:286: Allah does not burden beyond capacity
Hadith: every disease has a cure
Seeking help is part of tawakkul
teach.note: Cite plainly: Qur'an 2:286 and 94:5-6. Cite the hadith that Allah has not sent down a disease without sending down its cure (Bukhari). Explain that faith practices bring comfort and are part of a healthy routine, and that they go alongside talking to people and professional support when needed. Misconception: struggling means weak faith. Prophets experienced grief and hardship. Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass value of Resilience.

teach.heading: Building your support network
teach.note: Ask pupils to draw their personal support network without sharing names. Show how to reach Childline and Shout (text 85258, free 24/7). Practise a sentence to start a conversation. Explain that in an emergency or if someone is in immediate danger they should call 999. Remind pupils to follow up and tell another adult if the first does not help.

practice: Sort into helpful or unhelpful: (a) going for a walk (b) staying up all night scrolling (c) talking to a trusted adult (d) ignoring friends for weeks.
Write what you would say to a friend who has been withdrawn and tired for a month.
Name three people or services you can contact for support.
independent: Write a plan for Maryam with three helpful steps and the people who can support her.
Create a leaflet: ‘Looking after your mind’ with five strategies and two helplines.
Write a paragraph explaining how faith and seeking help work together.
exit: Give one helpful and one unhelpful way to cope.
Where can you get free, confidential support?
lessons.homework: Write three self-care activities you can do this week and which trusted adult you would talk to if worried.
lessons.send: SEND: use a visual traffic-light strategy sort and allow breaks. EAL: provide vocabulary for emotions. Stretch: evaluate three mental health websites for reliability.

lessons.title: Body image, media and self-worth
objectives: Explain how filters, advertising and social media can distort body image
Develop strategies for healthy self-esteem and critical media literacy
Link contentment and gratitude to self-worth

keywords.def: how you think and feel about your body
a tool that alters how a photo or video looks
a person who is paid to promote products online
how you value yourself
contentment with what Allah has given

starter: Bismillah. What is the difference between fact and opinion?
Name one way adverts persuade people.

teach.heading: What is body image?
bullets: How we see and feel about our bodies
Affected by family, friends and media
Boys and girls can both feel pressure
teach.note: Say bismillah. Define body image. Emphasise that many young people feel unsure about their appearance, and this is common. Discuss the pressure on boys (muscle, height) as well as girls. Do not use images of real people. Do not ask pupils to share their feelings about their bodies. Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass value of Contentment. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: What you see is not always real
bullets: Filters, editing and lighting change images
Influencers are paid to sell products
Ask: who gains if I feel unhappy?
teach.note: Show examples of edited images from stock or cartoon sources rather than real people. Explain that filters can change shape, skin and size. Ask pupils how they could check if an image is edited. Teach critical questions: Who made this? What do they want me to buy or believe? What is left out? Misconception: if lots of people look like that online, it must be normal.

teach.heading: Comparison and its effects
bullets: Unrealistic ideals can affect eating and exercise
Extreme diets and supplements can harm
Talk to a trusted adult or GP if worried
teach.note: Explain that comparing ourselves to edited images can make us feel worse. Mention that health professionals advise young people not to diet; they need a balanced intake to grow. Avoid details about eating disorders; simply state that worrying about food or weight that begins to take over is a reason to speak to a trusted adult or GP. Mention muscle-building supplements marketed to teenagers are not recommended.

teach.heading: Islamic teaching on worth and gratitude
bullets: Qur'an 95:4: created in the best of forms
Hadith: Allah looks at hearts and deeds
Shukr: be grateful for what you have
Real worth is character and taqwa
teach.note: Cite plainly: Qur'an 95:4 says that Allah created the human being in the best stature. Cite the hadith: Allah does not look at your appearance or wealth but at your hearts and deeds (Muslim). Link with Qur'an 49:13 on honour being linked to taqwa. Ask: ‘How is a person's worth measured?’ Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass value of Contentment (shukr).

teach.heading: Building healthy self-esteem
bullets: Focus on what your body can do
Limit time with accounts that make you feel bad
Spend time on strengths, faith and service
teach.note: Teach pupils to unfollow or mute accounts that harm their mood. Practise reframing: ‘I look wrong’ becomes ‘My body helps me pray, learn and play.’ Encourage gratitude lists and acts of service as boosts to self-worth. Remind pupils that the pastoral team is available for private chats. Close with a short du'a of thanks.

practice: Spot the clues that an image has been edited. Write three questions you could ask about it.
Rewrite this self-talk: ‘I will never look as good as him.’
True or false? (a) Everyone online looks the way they do in their posts. (b) Influencers are often paid. (c) Worth depends on appearance in Islam.
independent: Create a ‘Media detective’ checklist with five questions to ask about any image or advert.
Write a note to a younger pupil about being content and confident.
Write a paragraph explaining how Qur'an 95:4 and the hadith about hearts and deeds support healthy self-worth.
exit: Name two ways that images can be unrealistic.
Give one habit that builds healthy self-esteem.
lessons.homework: List three things your body helps you do and three things you are grateful for. Share one with a family member.
lessons.send: SEND: use cartoon or object examples for editing and visual prompt cards. EAL: pre-teach vocabulary with images. Stretch: research how advertisers use persuasion techniques and evaluate one advert.

lessons.title: Our class rules online; respect and difference
lessons.bigQuestion: In a live online lesson, what does respect look like when no one is in the same room?
objectives: To understand how respect for difference shapes the way we behave in an online community
successCriteria: All: state TGA's rules for live lessons and the class chat
Most: explain how respect applies to differences of background, ability and opinion
Some: agree a class charter and justify each rule
lessons.crossCurricular: Citizenship: British values of mutual respect and tolerance
lessons.smsc: Social and cultural: respect for diversity

keywords.def: treating others as valuable
ways people are not the same: background, language, ability, opinion
a set of agreed rules
good manners online

hook.text: In a live online lesson, what does respect look like when no one is in the same room?
hook.a: Cameras on, listening, kind chat, no screenshots of others, taking turns, valuing different views.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'O mankind, We created you from a male and a female and made you peoples and tribes so that you may know one another. The most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous' (al-Hujurat 49:13). Respect for every person comes from this.

starter.a: Democracy, rule of law, individual liberty, mutual respect, tolerance.
For example: education, safety, free speech within the law.
A duty we must carry out.

starter.q: Name one rule for our Teams chat.

teach.heading: TGA online rules
bullets: No recording or screenshots of others
teach.note: These rules protect privacy and learning.

teach.heading: Respecting difference
bullets: Disagree with ideas, never mock people
teach.note: Model respectful disagreement.

teach.heading: A class charter
teach.note: Model a rule with its reason.

model.problem: Turn 'don't be rude in the chat' into a charter rule.
steps: Reason: 'so everyone feels safe to ask'
model.answer: We type kind, helpful messages about the lesson, so everyone feels safe to ask.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: A classmate gives a wrong answer and someone types 'lol'. Best response?
options: Type something encouraging and tell the teacher if it continues
check.why: Upstanding kindly protects the learner; adults deal with repeated behaviour.

practice.q: Rewrite as a positive charter rule: 'No talking over people.'
practice.a: We take turns and let people finish speaking.
practice.model: Teacher rewrites positively and adds a reason.

independent.q: Core: Write five rules for our class charter with a reason for each (portal response box).
independent.a: Five positive, clear rules with reasons.
independent.model: Teacher writes rule 1 with its reason.

independent.q: Extend: Write how you would disagree respectfully with someone's view in a discussion.
independent.a: 'I understand your point; I see it differently because...'

independent.q: Stretch: Explain how al-Hujurat 49:13 supports respect for difference.
independent.a: Allah made people diverse so we know each other; nobility is by righteousness, not background.

exit.q: Netiquette means... A) online good manners B) a website C) a game
Big question: what does respect look like in a live online lesson?
exit.a: Cameras on, kind chat, listening, no screenshots, valuing difference.

lessons.homework: Share our class charter with your family and ask which rule they think matters most.
lessons.send: SEND: rule cards to choose from. EAL: respect, difference, rule. Stretch: compare our charter with British values.

lessons.title: Tackling racism and religious discrimination
lessons.bigQuestion: Have you ever been judged before someone knew you? How did it feel?
objectives: To understand what racism and religious discrimination are, how UK law protects people, and how to respond
successCriteria: All: define racism and religious discrimination
Most: name protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010
Some: explain how Islam's teaching on equality and UK law both oppose discrimination
lessons.crossCurricular: History: the Civil Rights movement and anti-discrimination law
lessons.smsc: Moral and cultural: equality and justice

keywords.def: treating people unfairly because of race, colour or ethnicity
treating someone unfairly because of who they are
the UK law protecting people from discrimination
a feature the Equality Act protects, such as race or religion

hook.text: Have you ever been judged before someone knew you? How did it feel?

islamicLink.text: In his Farewell Sermon the Prophet ﷺ taught that no Arab is better than a non-Arab, nor white better than black, except by taqwa (reported by Ahmad). Allah says the most noble are the most righteous (al-Hujurat 49:13). Bilal ibn Rabah, freed from slavery, was honoured to give the adhan.

starter.a: Someone who acts safely to help.
An unfair opinion formed without reason.

teach.heading: Definitions
bullets: Racism: unfair treatment due to race
Religious discrimination: due to faith or belief
teach.note: Respect for every person; discrimination against anyone is wrong.

teach.heading: The Equality Act 2010
bullets: Includes race and religion or belief
Illegal to discriminate at work, school, services
teach.note: Name them factually.

teach.heading: Responding
bullets: Report to school; the police for hate crimes
teach.note: Hate crimes can be reported to the police or True Vision (official reporting site).

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Refusing someone a job because of their religion is...
options: Discrimination, illegal under the Equality Act 2010
check.why: Religion or belief is a protected characteristic.

practice.a: For example: race, religion or belief, disability.
practice.model: Teacher names race and religion, linking to today's topic.

independent.q: Core: Case studies (pupil PDF, fictional): identify the discrimination, the protected characteristic and the right response.
Extend: In the portal response box, write a paragraph: 'Islam teaches equality because...'
independent.a: Islam teaches equality because Allah created all people and judges by righteousness, not race (49:13), as the Prophet ﷺ taught in the Farewell Sermon.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why protecting others' rights also protects Muslims' rights.
independent.a: The same law that protects others' beliefs protects ours; justice must be for all.

exit.q: The Equality Act 2010 protects... A) only adults B) nine characteristics including race and religion C) only football teams
exit.a: B) nine characteristics including race and religion
options: Nine characteristics including race and religion

exit.q: Big question: how should we respond to discrimination?
exit.a: Do not retaliate, record, report and support the target.

lessons.homework: Read about Bilal ibn Rabah and write three sentences on what his story teaches about equality.
lessons.send: SEND: definitions card. EAL: racism, discrimination, equality. Stretch: research the Race Relations Act 1965.

lessons.title: Making safe choices and saying no
lessons.bigQuestion: How do you decide quickly when something feels wrong?
objectives: To understand how to assess risk and make safe choices in everyday and online situations
successCriteria: All: identify risks in a situation
Most: use a decision-making model (stop, think, choose)
Some: plan an exit strategy and know who to contact

keywords.def: the chance of harm
what happens as a result of a choice
clear and respectful about what you will and will not do
a plan to leave a situation safely

hook.text: How do you decide quickly when something feels wrong?
hook.a: Trust the feeling, stop, think about consequences, choose the safe option.

islamicLink.text: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt' (at-Tirmidhi and an-Nasa'i). A believer checks their choices and thinks about consequences.

starter.q: Legal age to buy alcohol in the UK?

starter.a: The effect friends have on our choices.

starter.q: Name a trusted adult at TGA.

teach.heading: Spotting risk
teach.note: Fictional examples.

teach.heading: Stop, think, choose
teach.note: Model.

teach.heading: Being assertive
teach.note: Compare.

teach.heading: Exit strategies
bullets: Agree a code word with parents
Have a charged phone and a contact
Leave a group chat that turns bad
teach.note: Know: 999 for emergencies, 101 non-emergency police.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: An online friend you have never met asks to meet alone. Safest choice?
options: Say no and tell a parent
Go with a friend your age
check.why: People online may not be who they say; a parent must know and decide.

practice.q: Use stop, think, choose for: 'A friend dares you to cross a busy road.'
practice.a: Stop; risk of injury; choose to refuse and walk to a crossing.

independent.q: Core: Risk scenarios (pupil PDF): apply stop, think, choose to each and write an exit strategy.
Extend: In the portal response box, write a reflection: who would you talk to after a risky situation, and why?
independent.a: Names a trusted adult and explains they can help.

exit.q: Assertive means... A) shouting B) clear, calm and respectful C) agreeing to everything
Big question: how do you decide quickly when something feels wrong?
exit.a: Stop, think about consequences, choose the safe option, tell someone.

lessons.homework: Agree a code word with your parents for when you need to leave a situation.
lessons.send: SEND: stop, think, choose card. EAL: risk, consequence, assertive. Stretch: research when to call 999 or 101.
